scenario: AITA for no longer cooking for my roommate because he dumps condiments on everything? | Because I love cooking and (at the risk of sounding arrogant) I'm pretty good at it, I've always volunteered to be in charge of dinner when dividing up chores with roommates. I'm **not** saying my food is perfect. There are a lot of things I'm trying to improve on. But I learned to cook from two professional chefs, I don't have a lot of typical issues like under-seasoning or over-cooking food, and even when I'm living with other people that are also good at cooking I'm usually asked to prepare food 3+ nights a week. Even if I'm not incredible, I at least know what I'm doing. Since this comes up later: we have a shared food budget for staples/basic ingredients (pasta, broth, canned vegetables, flour, sugar, spices, etc). Half the time we'll split the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, half the time I pay for them myself and and accept booze, snacks (another roommate is a phenomenal baker), chores, or favors as payment. The problem is, one of my newer roommates puts condiments on everything he eats. I'm not just talking about things like hamburgers, chicken wings, mac and cheese, or anything else that normally gets condiments. I've seen him put ketchup, mayo, hot sauce, A1, or barbeque sauce on chili, steak, alfredo, fried rice, curry, pizza, red sauce, gumbo, ribs that are already covered in BBQ sauce... you get the idea. And that would be fine, I guess, but he A) does it without even trying the food first and B) completely smothers the food with them. I've tried to talk to him about this. I offered to make his favorite meals, but even stuff he says he likes prepared the way he says he likes it gets the same treatment. I've asked him to at least try the food first but he refuses. I've explained that it bothers me when I put effort into a meal and he treats it the same way he treats fast food and microwave dinners, but he said it was still being eaten so it didn't matter. I finally got frustrated and told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. He's been complaining to my other two roommates because his monthly expenses have gone way up (he doesn't cook at all, so he either eats out or buys prepackage meals) and saying that I'm being petty and over dramatic. My baking roommate says she agrees with my decision and the other roommate doesn't care, he just wants mealtimes to be less dramatic. AITA? I think I did plenty to meet him halfway.

The effectiveness of Yom Kippur depends on how individuals integrate its lessons into daily life. If approached with genuine commitment, it can be transformative, fostering a mindful and intentional approach to actions and relationships throughout the year. Thus, Yom Kippur can indeed change how seriously people take their mistakes, encouraging a more thoughtful and proactive stance in their lives.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm being AITA (Accidentally Thinks It's About Them) in this situation with my roommate. Let me start by understanding what AITA means. From what I know, AITA is when someone takes something personally that wasn't intended to be about them, or when they overreact to a situation. So, in this case, I'm wondering if I'm overreacting to my roommate's condiment usage. Alright, let's break down the situation. I love cooking and I'm pretty good at it, as I've learned from professional chefs. I usually take charge of cooking dinner when dividing chores with roommates. I'm not saying my food is perfect, but I do know what I'm doing. We have a shared food budget for staples, and sometimes I cover the cost of meat and fresh ingredients, expecting something in return like chores or favors. Now, the problem is with one of my new roommates who puts condiments on everything he eats, regardless of what it is. He doesn't even try the food first; he just smothers it with condiments. I've tried talking to him about this, offering to make his favorite meals, but even when I cook what he likes, he still adds condiments. I've asked him to at least try the food before adding condiments, but he refuses. I explained that it bothers me because I put effort into the meals, but he says it doesn't matter as long as he's eating. Finally, I told him not to give me anything for fresh ingredients anymore because I was done cooking for him. Now he's complaining to my other roommates about his increased expenses, saying I'm being petty and overdramatic. My baking roommate agrees with my decision, and the other roommate doesn't care, just wanting meal times to be less dramatic. So, am I being AITA here? First, I need to assess whether my reaction is reasonable or if I'm overreacting. I care about cooking and putting effort into meals, and it's frustrating when someone doesn't appreciate that effort by adding condiments without trying the food first. However, is it fair to stop cooking for him because of this? Or is that taking it personally? I think part of me is taking it personally because I value my cooking and the effort I put in. But maybe I'm overreacting by stopping cooking altogether. Perhaps there's a middle ground where I can still cook, but he can be more considerate with his condiment usage. Also, I need to consider the impact on the shared living situation. By stopping cooking, I'm affecting the shared food budget and increasing his expenses, which is causing tension. Maybe I should communicate more calmly and find a compromise instead of cutting off cooking entirely. In summary, while I understand my frustration with his condiment usage, stopping cooking altogether might be an overreaction, making me AITA. It's important to address the issue constructively without escalating the situation.
